claims.text: A multiobjective optimization model is developed to simultaneously maximize spectrum efficiency and energy efficiency in UAV-assisted cellular networks under specific constraints, and a compositive efficiency metric is introduced to transform the multiobjective optimization problem into a single-objective optimization problem for efficient Pareto solution determination.

A centralized Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) based Dueling Deep Q-Network (DDQN) algorithm with Mish activation function is proposed to improve exploration efficiency and accelerate convergence in solving the joint beamforming and power allocation problem in UAV-assisted cellular networks.

A federated UCB DDQN learning framework is introduced to address the challenges of excessive data exchange and privacy concerns in centralized deep reinforcement learning by enabling decentralized collaborative learning and model aggregation without sharing raw data.

Simulation results demonstrate that the UCB DDQN-based joint beamforming and power allocation approach achieves higher total weighted energy-spectrum efficiency and faster convergence compared to conventional DQN-based methods.

The federated UCB DDQN implementation outperforms the centralized UCB DDQN in terms of total weighted energy-spectrum efficiency, demonstrating the benefits of federated deep reinforcement learning in UAV-assisted cellular networks.

similar_papers.title: Optimization Theory-Based Deep Reinforcement Learning for Resource Allocation in Ultra-Reliable Wireless Networked Control Systems
similar_papers.abstract: The design of Wireless Networked Control System (WNCS) requires addressing critical interactions between control and communication systems with minimal complexity and communication overhead while providing ultra-high reliability. This paper introduces a novel optimization theory based deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework for the joint design of controller and communication systems. The objective of minimum power consumption is targeted while satisfying the schedulability and rate constraints of the communication system in the finite blocklength regime and stability constraint of the control system. Decision variables include the sampling period in the control system, and blocklength and packet error probability in the communication system. The proposed framework contains two stages: optimization theory and DRL. In the optimization theory stage, following the formulation of the joint optimization problem, optimality conditions are derived to find the mathematical relations between the optimal values of the decision variables. These relations allow the decomposition of the problem into multiple building blocks. In the DRL stage, the blocks that are simplified but not tractable are replaced by DRL. Via extensive simulations, the proposed optimization theory based DRL approach is demonstrated to outperform the optimization theory and pure DRL based approaches, with close to optimal performance and much lower complexity.

claims.text: An optimization theory-based deep reinforcement learning framework enables joint optimization of control and communication systems in wireless networked control systems, minimizing power consumption while ensuring ultra-reliable transmission in the finite blocklength regime.

The proposed framework decomposes the optimization problem into multiple building blocks using derived optimality conditions, simplifying the problem and reducing decision variables to blocklength while replacing intractable components with deep reinforcement learning models.

The optimization theory-based deep reinforcement learning approach outperforms pure deep reinforcement learning methods and achieves near-optimal performance compared to conventional optimization theory methods, with significantly lower complexity and reduced training data requirements.

The framework incorporates stochastic maximum allowed transfer interval and maximum allowed packet delay constraints to ensure control system stability while optimizing communication system parameters such as sampling period, blocklength, and packet error probability.

The proposed deep reinforcement learning algorithms, including DQN and DDQN, demonstrate robustness and adaptability in dynamic environments, achieving efficient resource allocation in wireless networked control systems across varying network sizes and constraints.

similar_papers.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning Based Resource Allocation Approach for Wireless Networks Considering Network Slicing Paradigm
similar_papers.abstract: In this paper, we present an approach for resource scheduling in wireless networks based on the Network Slicing (NS) paradigm using Double Deep Q-Network (DDQN) Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithm. More specifically, we propose a joint power and Scheduling Block (SB) allocation algorithm for networks with NS. The reinforcement learning algorithm applied to the resource allocation problem is formulated using state transitions regarding the system dynamics. We also present an algorithm, namely Network Slicing based on Reinforcement Learning (NSRL) that combines the proposed reinforcement learning based resource allocation with an approach based on reservation and sharing of resources among the slices where each RL agent acts in one slice. Simulations are carried out considering User Equipments (UEs) within a small cell coverage area - (Small Cells) with different Modulation and Coding Schemes (MCS) standardized by the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) based on a simplified NS scenario with fifth generation wireless network (5G) characteristics. In the simulations, two slices are considered for the UEs: one considering Ultra-reliable and Low Latency Communications (URLLC) and other related to enhanced Mobile Broadband (eMBB) services. Simulation results show that the NSRL algorithm efficiently allocates power and SBs, outperforming other algorithms in the literature.

The relationship between the probability of successful packet transmission (PSPT) and signal transmission power can be accurately modeled using sigmoidal functions for different Channel Quality Indicators (CQIs) standardized by 3GPP, with parameters estimated using the Levenberg-Marquardt nonlinear curve fitting method.

The Network Slicing based on Reinforcement Learning (NSRL) algorithm combines reinforcement learning with resource reservation and sharing strategies to efficiently allocate power and scheduling blocks among slices, enhancing Quality of Service (QoS) for eMBB and URLLC services.

Reward functions tailored for eMBB and URLLC slices enable reinforcement learning agents to optimize throughput for eMBB services and minimize delay while maximizing reliability for URLLC services without prior knowledge of system statistics.

The NSRL algorithm with DDQN agents outperforms traditional algorithms like Distributed Algorithm (DA) and Equal Sharing (ES) in terms of packet transmission delay, throughput, energy efficiency, and processing time in network slicing scenarios.

similar_papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Techniques for Joint Power and Delay Optimization Based Resource Allocation in MIMO-OFDM System Using Deep Convolutional Red Piranha Pyramid-Dilated Neural Network: Trends and Challenges
similar_papers.abstract: The rapid development of 6G wireless communication systems demands intelligent resource allocation strategies capable of optimizing both power consumption and transmission delay in MU-MIMO-OFDM environments. Traditional optimization techniques struggle with highdimensional decision spaces, dynamic channel conditions, and stringent Quality of Service (QoS) requirements. Recently, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven approaches, particularly deep learning and hybrid optimization models, have shown significant potential in addressing these challenges. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of AIbased techniques for joint power and delay optimization in MIMO-OFDM systems, focusing on advanced architectures such as Deep Convolutional Pyramid-Dilated Neural Networks (DCPDNN) integrated with metaheuristic algorithms like Red Piranha Optimization. The proposed frameworks enable efficient resource allocation by jointly optimizing transmission power, subcarrier assignment, and delay scheduling. Recent studies demonstrate improvements in throughput, energy efficiency, and latency reduction through multi-stage optimization strategies. Furthermore, reinforcement learning, graph neural networks, and transformer-based scheduling methods are explored as emerging solutions for adaptive resource management. A systematic review of recent literature (2020–2023) highlights trends, performance trade-offs, and research gaps. The survey concludes with future directions emphasizing scalable, energy-efficient, and secure AI-driven wireless communication systems for next-generation networks.

similar_papers.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning Based Resource Allocation for Cloud Native Wireless Network
similar_papers.abstract: Cloud native technology has revolutionized 5G beyond and 6G communication networks, offering unprecedented levels of operational automation, flexibility, and adaptability. However, the vast array of cloud native services and applications presents a new challenge in resource allocation for dynamic cloud computing environments. To tackle this challenge, we investigate a cloud native wireless architecture that employs container-based virtualization to enable flexible service deployment. We then study two representative use cases: network slicing and Multi-Access Edge Computing. To optimize resource allocation in these scenarios, we leverage deep reinforcement learning techniques and introduce two model-free algorithms capable of monitoring the network state and dynamically training allocation policies. We validate the effectiveness of our algorithms in a testbed developed using Free5gc. Our findings demonstrate significant improvements in network efficiency, underscoring the potential of our proposed techniques in unlocking the full potential of cloud native wireless networks.

A TD3-based algorithm effectively allocates bandwidth among network slices by maximizing a utility function derived from latency, transmission rate, and service type.
A DQN-based algorithm minimizes task processing latency in Multi-Access Edge Computing networks by optimizing task offloading strategies among edge servers and the core network.

similar_papers.title: Semantic-Aware Resource Allocation Based on Deep Reinforcement Learning for 5G-V2X HetNets
similar_papers.abstract: This letter proposes a semantic-aware resource allocation (SARA) framework with flexible duty cycle (DC) coexistence mechanism (SARADC) for 5G-V2X Heterogeneous Network (HetNets) based on deep reinforcement learning (DRL) proximal policy optimization (PPO). Specifically, we investigate V2X networks within a three-tiered HetNets structure. To meet the demands of high-speed vehicular networking in urban environments, we design a semantic communication system and introduce two resource allocation metrics: high-speed semantic transmission rate (HSR) and semantic spectrum efficiency (HSSE). Additionally, we address the coexistence of vehicular users and WiFi users in 5G New Radio Unlicensed (NR-U) networks. Our approach jointly optimizes the DC coexistence mechanism and the allocation of resources and base stations (BSs). Unlike traditional bit-based transmission methods, our approach integrates the semantic communication into the communication system. Experimental results show that our proposed framework significantly improves HSSE and semantic throughput (ST) for both vehicular and WiFi users compared to conventional methods.

The proposed framework integrates semantic communication into vehicular networks, introducing novel metrics such as high-speed semantic transmission rate and semantic spectrum efficiency to optimize resource allocation and base station usage.

The framework addresses coexistence challenges between vehicular users and WiFi users in 5G New Radio Unlicensed networks by jointly optimizing duty cycle coexistence mechanisms and resource allocation.
The use of semantic communication in resource allocation enhances spectrum efficiency and reduces congestion compared to traditional bit-based methods in vehicular networks.

The semantic-aware resource allocation framework demonstrates superior performance in terms of semantic spectrum efficiency and semantic throughput for both vehicular and WiFi users compared to conventional methods, particularly when data is encoded with more than 8 bits per word.

similar_papers.title: Energy Efficiency and Throughput Optimization in Massive MIMO Systems Using Deep Reinforcement Learning
similar_papers.abstract:
The importance of Massive Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (Massive MIMO) technology is an
essential feature of today 5G and the future 6G wireless communication like it is capable of making
the differences in spectral efficiency, network capacity, and the number of users it can serve
significant. Based on joint optimization of energy efficiency (EE) and system throughput, also
known as spectral efficiency (SE) is a problem that is difficult to address due to high-dimensional
state space, dynamic channel conditions, inter-user interference, and hard power constraints.
Conventional optimization models which include convex optimization and heuristic scheduling
algorithms do not lend themselves well to the fast-paced conditions of wireless networks and a large
number of antennas. This paper suggests a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)-based optimization
system that can enhance energy efficiency and throughput in Massive MIMO systems
simultaneously. The resource allocation problem is called a Markov Decision Process (MDP) in
which the agent learns the optimal policies to deal with beamforming, power distribution, antenna
activation, and user scheduling by interacting with the network environment. The framework mainly
uses the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm and is compared to the traditional methods
of convex optimization and heuristic baselines. Large-scale simulations were carried out based on
Rayleigh fading channel models, realistic base station-user topologies and antenna configurations
up to 64 to 512 antennas. The results of the experiments prove that the proposed DRL framework
plays a significant role in enhancing the performance of the network. As an example, a DRL model
with 128 antennas had 8.5 bits/Joule energy efficiency and 8.2 bps/Hz spectral efficiency, compared
to 6.7 bits/Joule and 6.1 bps/Hz with convex optimization. The difference in throughput between
different levels of user density increased by 15-25 percent and the QoS violation rates were kept at
below 1 percent and inference latency at less than 5 ms, which allowed real-time deployment. In
general, the findings establish that DRL offers a scalable and adaptive optimization strategy that is
efficient in balancing energy usage and throughput in large-scale wireless networks. The given
framework is a step in the direction of the creation of self-optimizing, energy-conscious intelligent
communication systems of the next-generation 6G networks.

The DRL-based framework demonstrates scalability and adaptability across varying antenna configurations (32 to 512 antennas) and user densities (5 to 25 users), maintaining low Quality of Service (QoS) violation rates below 1% and inference latency under 5 milliseconds.

The DRL framework outperforms traditional convex optimization and heuristic methods in energy efficiency and spectral efficiency, achieving better throughput and resource utilization under dynamic channel conditions and imperfect channel state information.

The proposed DRL model effectively balances the trade-off between energy efficiency and spectral efficiency by integrating both metrics into a unified reward function, enabling adaptive and context-aware optimization in Massive MIMO systems.

The DRL-based optimization system is robust to dynamic wireless environments, including user mobility and channel fading, due to its ability to generalize policies learned during training and adapt to stochastic variations in real-time.

similar_papers.title: Latency and Energy Minimization in NOMA-Assisted MEC Network: A Federated Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach
similar_papers.abstract: Multi-access edge computing (MEC) is seen as a vital component of forthcoming 6G wireless networks, aiming to support emerging applications that demand high service reliability and low latency. However, ensuring the ultra-reliable and low-latency performance of MEC networks poses a significant challenge due to uncertainties associated with wireless links, constraints imposed by communication and computing resources, and the dynamic nature of network traffic. Enabling ultra-reliable and low-latency MEC mandates efficient load balancing jointly with resource allocation. In this paper, we investigate the joint optimization problem of offloading decisions, computation and communication resource allocation to minimize the expected weighted sum of delivery latency and energy consumption in a non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA)-assisted MEC network. Given the formulated problem is a mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP), a new multi-agent federated deep reinforcement learning (FDRL) solution based on double deep Q-network (DDQN) is developed to efficiently optimize the offloading strategies across the MEC network while accelerating the learning process of the Internet-of-Thing (IoT) devices. Simulation results show that the proposed FDRL scheme can effectively reduce the weighted sum of delivery latency and energy consumption of IoT devices in the MEC network and outperform the baseline approaches.

claims.text: A federated deep reinforcement learning (FDRL) framework based on double deep Q-network (DDQN) can effectively optimize offloading decisions, base station assignment, and channel resource allocation in non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA)-assisted multi-access edge computing (MEC) networks, minimizing the weighted sum of delivery latency and energy consumption for Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices.

The integration of federated learning (FL) into the double deep Q-network (DDQN) framework enhances the scalability, privacy, and learning speed of IoT devices in multi-access edge computing (MEC) networks by enabling decentralized training and global model aggregation.

The proposed federated deep reinforcement learning (FDRL) algorithm outperforms baseline approaches in reducing delivery latency and energy consumption in NOMA-assisted MEC networks under various system parameters, including computing frequency, bandwidth allocation, and network size.

The proposed optimization framework addresses the joint problem of offloading decisions, computing resource allocation, and transmit power control in NOMA-assisted MEC networks, ensuring ultra-reliable low-latency communication and meeting strict quality-of-service (QoS) requirements for IoT devices.

The federated deep reinforcement learning (FDRL) approach provides a privacy-preserving and efficient solution to the mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP) problem of resource allocation in multi-access edge computing (MEC) networks, leveraging local training and global model aggregation to optimize network performance.

similar_papers.title: Anti-Jamming Resource Allocation for Integrated Sensing and Communications Based on Game-Guided Reinforcement Learning
similar_papers.abstract: Jamming attacks severely degrade both the sensing and communication performances, and thus this letter investigates the problem of anti-jamming resource allocation optimization in integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems. Our objective is to maximize the weighted sum of the communication rate and the effective sensing power while meeting both communication and sensing requirements against malicious jamming. Since the joint optimization of communication and sensing is a highly coupled problem as well as the jamming behavior is dynamic, we then propose an advanced game-guided deep reinforcement learning (DRL) algorithm to address the resource allocation issue. Specifically, the power control problem is modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), while the channel selection problem is formulated as a Stackelberg game. We further prove the existence of a Stackelberg equilibrium (SE). Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed DRL-based-anti-jamming approach significantly enhances the communication and sensing performances of ISAC systems compared to other baseline methods, supporting superior resistance to inter-channel interference (ICI) and jamming attacks.

claims.text: An advanced Stackelberg game-guided deep reinforcement learning (G-DDPG) algorithm can effectively optimize channel selection and power control in integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems to maximize the weighted sum of communication rate and effective sensing power while mitigating the impact of malicious jamming and inter-channel interference.

The power control problem in ISAC systems can be modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), and the channel selection problem can be formulated as a Stackelberg game, with the existence of a unique Stackelberg equilibrium (SE) proven for the proposed framework.

The proposed G-DDPG-based anti-jamming approach demonstrates superior performance in terms of communication and sensing capabilities compared to baseline methods, achieving higher rewards and better resistance to jamming and inter-channel interference.

The proposed G-DDPG algorithm outperforms traditional beamforming-only approaches in both underloaded and overloaded ISAC scenarios by optimizing device channel selection and base station transmit power, resulting in improved sensing resolution and communication quality.

The integration of a Stackelberg game with deep reinforcement learning provides a robust framework for adaptive anti-jamming strategies in ISAC systems, ensuring optimal and stable responses to dynamic jammer behavior.

similar_papers.title: Graph Neural Networks and Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Resource Allocation for V2X Communications
similar_papers.abstract: In the rapidly evolving landscape of Internet of Vehicles (IoV) technology, cellular vehicle-to-everything (C-V2X) communication has attracted much attention due to its superior performance in coverage, latency, and throughput. Resource allocation within C-V2X is crucial for ensuring the transmission of safety information and meeting the stringent requirements for ultralow latency and high reliability in vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication. This article proposes a method that integrates graph neural networks (GNNs) with deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to address this challenge. By constructing a dynamic graph with communication links as nodes and employing the graph sample and aggregation (GraphSAGE) model to adapt to changes in graph structure, the model aims to ensure a high success rate for V2V communication while minimizing interference on vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) links, thereby ensuring the successful transmission of V2V link information and maintaining high transmission rates for V2I links. The proposed method retains the global feature learning capabilities of GNN and supports distributed network deployment, allowing vehicles to extract low-dimensional features that include structural information from the graph network based on local observations and to make independent resource allocation decisions. Simulation results indicate that the introduction of GNN, with a modest increase in computational load, effectively enhances the decision-making quality of agents, demonstrating superiority to other methods. This study not only provides a theoretically efficient resource allocation strategy for V2V and V2I communications but also paves a new technical path for resource management in practical IoV environments.

claims.text: Integrating Graph Neural Networks with Deep Reinforcement Learning enables distributed resource allocation in Cellular Vehicle-to-Everything communication systems, allowing vehicles to extract low-dimensional features from local observations and make independent decisions while maintaining high V2V communication success rates and minimizing interference to V2I links.

The Graph Sample and Aggregate model adapts to dynamic graph structures in vehicular networks by sampling neighbors and incorporating edge weights, enabling efficient feature extraction and reducing computational complexity compared to complete graph methods.

The proposed graph construction method based on communication relationships limits the number of neighbors per node, ensuring stable computational load and preserving strong interference relationships in high-density vehicular environments.

Combining Graph Neural Networks with Double Deep Q-Networks improves resource allocation strategies in vehicular networks by leveraging global structural information and optimizing channel and power selection to meet latency and reliability requirements for V2V links while enhancing V2I transmission rates.

The GNN-DDQN framework demonstrates robustness in dynamic vehicular environments, maintaining stable V2V communication success rates and adapting to fluctuating vehicle densities while minimizing interference to V2I links.

similar_papers.title: Optimisation of Resource Allocation in Heterogeneous Wireless Networks Using Deep Reinforcement Learning
similar_papers.abstract: Dynamic resource allocation in open radio access network (O-RAN) heterogeneous networks (HetNets) presents a complex optimisation challenge under varying user loads. We propose a near-real-time RAN intelligent controller (NearRT RIC) xApp utilising deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to jointly optimise transmit power, bandwidth slicing, and user scheduling. Leveraging real-world network topologies, we benchmark proximal policy optimisation (PPO) and twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3) against standard heuristics. Our results demonstrate that the PPO-based xApp achieves a superior trade-off, reducing network energy consumption by up to 70 % in dense scenarios and improving user fairness by more than 30 % compared to throughput-greedy baselines. These findings validate the feasibility of centralised, energy-aware AI orchestration in future 6 G architectures.

claims.text: A near-real-time RAN intelligent controller (Near-RT RIC) xApp utilizing deep reinforcement learning optimizes transmit power, bandwidth slicing, and user scheduling in heterogeneous wireless networks, achieving significant improvements in energy efficiency and user fairness compared to heuristic baselines.

Proximal policy optimization (PPO) demonstrates superior performance in balancing energy consumption, throughput, and fairness in dense urban and mixed network scenarios, outperforming twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3) and traditional heuristic methods.

The proposed Markov decision process (MDP) formulation for O-RAN xApps integrates global channel knowledge and realistic interference geometries, enabling effective resource allocation in heterogeneous wireless networks.

Deep reinforcement learning algorithms such as PPO and TD3 are validated as feasible for deployment in O-RAN architectures, meeting near-real-time constraints while optimizing multi-objective utility functions for throughput, fairness, and energy efficiency.

Simulation results using real-world base station coordinates confirm that PPO-based xApps achieve up to 70% energy reduction and over 30% improvement in user fairness compared to throughput-greedy baselines in heterogeneous wireless networks.

similar_papers.title: Federated Deep Reinforcement Learning for Online Task Offloading and Resource Allocation in WPC-MEC Networks
similar_papers.abstract: Mobile edge computing (MEC) is considered a more effective new technological solution for developing the Internet of Things (IoT) by providing cloud-like capabilities for mobile users. This article combines wireless powered communication (WPC) technology with an MEC network, where a base station (BS) can transfer wireless energy to edge users (EUs) and execute computation-intensive tasks through task offloading. Traditional numerical optimization methods are time-consuming approaches for solving this problem in time-varying wireless channels, and centralized deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is not stable in large-scale dynamic IoT networks. Therefore, we propose a federated DRL-based online task offloading and resource allocation (FDOR) algorithm. In this algorithm, DRL is executed in EUs, and federated learning (FL) uses the distributed architecture of MEC to aggregate and update the parameters. To further solve the problem of the non-IID data of mobile EUs, we devise an adaptive method that automatically adjusts the FDOR algorithm’s learning rate. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed FDOR algorithm is superior to the traditional numerical optimization method and the existing DRL algorithm in four aspects: convergence speed, execution delay, overall calculation rate and stability in large-scale and dynamic IoT.

claims.text: A federated deep reinforcement learning-based algorithm for online task offloading and resource allocation in wireless powered communication-enabled mobile edge computing networks improves the overall computation rate and reduces execution latency by distributing the deep reinforcement learning model to edge users for local training and aggregating parameters using federated learning.

An adaptive learning rate method mitigates the impact of non-independent and identically distributed data on federated learning in mobile edge computing networks, ensuring faster convergence and stable performance in dynamic and large-scale environments.

The federated deep reinforcement learning-based algorithm maintains stability and low computational delay in large-scale dynamic mobile edge computing networks, outperforming traditional numerical optimization methods and existing deep reinforcement learning algorithms in terms of convergence speed, execution delay, and overall calculation rate.

The proposed federated deep reinforcement learning algorithm effectively addresses challenges in dynamic mobile edge computing networks, such as frequent user equipment on/off events and varying task computation cycles, by leveraging distributed training and adaptive learning rate adjustments.

The federated deep reinforcement learning-based algorithm achieves near-optimal performance in computation rate and execution latency, demonstrating scalability and robustness in wireless powered communication-enabled mobile edge computing networks with up to 50 edge users.

similar_papers.title: Joint Admission Control and Resource Allocation of Virtual Network Embedding via Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning
similar_papers.abstract: As an essential resource management problem in network virtualization, virtual network embedding (VNE) aims to allocate the finite resources of physical network to sequentially arriving virtual network requests (VNRs) with different resource demands. Since this is an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem, many efforts have been made to provide viable solutions. However, most existing approaches have either ignored the admission control of VNRs, which has a potential impact on long-term performances, or not fully exploited the temporal and topological features of the physical network and VNRs. In this article, we propose a deep Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning approach to learn a joint Admission Control and Resource Allocation policy for VNE, named HRL-ACRA. Specifically, the whole VNE process is decomposed into an upper-level policy for deciding whether to admit the arriving VNR or not and a lower-level policy for allocating resources of the physical network to meet the requirement of VNR through the HRL approach. Considering the proximal policy optimization as the basic training algorithm, we also adopt the average reward method to address the infinite horizon problem of the upper-level agent and design a customized multi-objective intrinsic reward to alleviate the sparse reward issue of the lower-level agent. Moreover, we develop a deep feature-aware graph neural network to capture the features of VNR and physical network and exploit a sequence-to-sequence model to generate embedding actions iteratively. Finally, extensive experiments are conducted in various settings, and show that HRL-ACRA outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of both the acceptance ratio and long-term average revenue.

claims.text: A hierarchical reinforcement learning framework named HRL-ACRA is proposed to jointly optimize admission control and resource allocation for virtual network embedding, where the upper-level agent decides whether to admit incoming virtual network requests and the lower-level agent allocates resources to admitted requests.

The HRL-ACRA framework employs a customized graph neural network to extract topological and resource features of physical and virtual networks, and a sequence-to-sequence model with a gated recurrent unit-based decoder to iteratively generate resource allocation solutions.

The upper-level agent in HRL-ACRA uses the average reward method to address the infinite horizon problem and incorporates a penalty mechanism to reject infeasible virtual network requests, thereby improving long-term resource utilization and revenue.

The lower-level agent in HRL-ACRA utilizes a multi-objective intrinsic reward function that balances revenue-to-cost ratio and resource load balancing to guide efficient exploration and improve the quality of resource allocation solutions.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that HRL-ACRA outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of acceptance ratio and long-term average revenue across various network scenarios, including different arrival rates, resource demands, and real-world network topologies.

similar_papers.title: Applying Machine Learning to Optimize Resource Allocation & Maritime Wireless Mobile Network
similar_papers.abstract:
Resource allocation in dynamic maritime wireless mobile networks is essential for uninterrupted
communication due to the complexities posed by the marine environment. Traditional methods of
resource allocation still fail to address the challenges posed by bandwidth variability, mobility
patterns, and coverage areas even with strong technological advancement. This research is
concerned with the optimization of resource allocation processes in wireless mobile networks using
machine learning (ML) algorithms to increase reliability, throughput, and reduce latency. Various
machine learning algorithms including supervised learning and reinforcement learning were
analysed using real and simulated datasets from the maritime domain. This study focuses on creating
the experimental design for training and validating the models with the golden metrics of packet
delivery ratio, spectral efficiency, and network utilization. Results show that ML resource allocation
strategies automate and anticipate dynamic changes, allowing for better resource allocation
adaptability, therefore significantly outperforming traditional techniques. The results indicate that
there is great potential for improving the maritime communication infrastructure through intelligent
solutions. This study serves as a guide and basic framework for future monitoring and research in
maritime networking for real world applications.

similar_papers.title: Priority-Aware Resource Allocation for VNF Deployment in Service Function Chains Based on Graph Reinforcement Learning
similar_papers.abstract: : Recently, Network Functions Virtualization (NFV) has become a critical resource for optimizing capability utilization in the 5G/B5G era. NFV decomposes the network resource paradigm, demonstrating the efficient utilization of Network Functions (NFs) to enable configurable service priorities and resource demands. Telecommunications Service Providers (TSPs) face challenges in network utilization, as the vast amounts of data generated by the Internet of Things (IoT) overwhelm existing infrastructures. IoT applications, which generate massive volumes of diverse data and require real-time communication, contribute to bottlenecks and congestion. In this context, Multi-access Edge Computing (MEC) is employed to support resource and priority-aware IoT applications by implementing Virtual Network Function (VNF) sequences within Service Function Chaining (SFC). This paper proposes the use of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) combined with Graph Neural Networks (GNN) to enhance network processing, performance, and resource pooling capabilities. GNN facilitates feature extraction through Message-Passing Neural Network (MPNN) mechanisms. Together with DRL, Deep Q-Networks (DQN) are utilized to dynamically allocate resources based on IoT network priorities and demands. Our focus is on minimizing delay times for VNF instance execution, ensuring effective resource placement, and allocation in SFC deployments, offering flexibility to adapt to real-time changes in priority and workload. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed scheme outperforms reference models in terms of reward, delay, delivery, service drop ratios, and average completion ratios, proving its potential for IoT applications.

claims.text: A priority-aware resource allocation framework for Virtual Network Function (VNF) deployment in Multi-access Edge Computing (MEC) environments integrates Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) with Graph Neural Networks (GNN) to optimize Service Function Chain (SFC) placement and resource utilization based on service priorities in IoT networks.

The proposed Priority-Aware VNF Deployment Algorithm (PVD-GDR) leverages a GNN-based Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) for feature extraction and a Deep Q-Network (DQN) for dynamic resource orchestration, ensuring efficient resource allocation and adaptive decision-making in real-time IoT applications.

The PVD-GDR framework minimizes delay and resource usage while maximizing the SFC acceptance ratio by dynamically adapting to workload and priority changes in IoT networks, ensuring Quality of Service (QoS) for critical applications.

The integration of GNN and DRL in the PVD-GDR framework enables scalable and efficient handling of non-Euclidean data in network topologies, improving task placement and resource efficiency in MEC-enabled IoT environments.

Simulation results demonstrate that the PVD-GDR framework outperforms traditional load-balancing, greedy, and Deep Q-Learning (DQL) approaches in terms of cumulative reward, task execution delay, delivery ratio, task drop ratio, and average completion ratio for IoT service requests.

similar_papers.title: PandORA: Automated Design and Comprehensive Evaluation of Deep Reinforcement Learning Agents for Open RAN
similar_papers.abstract: The highly heterogeneous ecosystem of Next Generation (NextG) wireless communication systems calls for novel networking paradigms where functionalities and operations can be dynamically and optimally reconfigured in real time to adapt to changing traffic conditions and satisfy stringent and diverse Quality of Service (QoS) demands. Open Radio Access Network (RAN) technologies, and specifically those being standardized by the O-RAN Alliance, make it possible to integrate network intelligence into the once monolithic RAN via intelligent applications, namely, xApps and rApps. These applications enable flexible control of the network resources and functionalities, network management, and orchestration through data-driven intelligent control loops. Recent work has showed how Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) is effective in dynamically controlling O-RAN systems. However, how to design these solutions in a way that manages heterogeneous optimization goals and prevents unfair resource allocation is still an open challenge, with the logic within DRL agents often considered as a opaque system. In this paper, we introduce PandORA, a framework to automatically design and train DRL agents for Open RAN applications, package them as xApps and evaluate them in the Colosseum wireless network emulator. We benchmark 23 xApps that embed DRL agents trained using different architectures, reward design, action spaces, and decision-making timescales, and with the ability to hierarchically control different network parameters. We test these agents on the Colosseum testbed under diverse traffic and channel conditions, in static and mobile setups. Our experimental results indicate how suitable fine-tuning of the RAN control timers, as well as proper selection of reward designs and DRL architectures can boost network performance according to the network conditions and demand. Notably, finer decision-making granularities can improve Massive Machine-Type Communications (mMTC)’s performance by <inline-formula><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\sim\! 56\%$</tex-math><alternatives><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="-0.166667em"/><mml:mn>56</mml:mn><mml:mo>%</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math><inline-graphic xlink:href="tsampazi-ieq1-3505781.gif"/></alternatives></inline-formula> and even increase Enhanced Mobile Broadband (eMBB) Throughput by <inline-formula><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\sim\! 99\%$</tex-math><alternatives><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="-0.166667em"/><mml:mn>99</mml:mn><mml:mo>%</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math><inline-graphic xlink:href="tsampazi-ieq2-3505781.gif"/></alternatives></inline-formula>.

claims.text: The PandORA framework automates the design, training, and evaluation of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agents for Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) applications, enabling the deployment of xApps for near-real-time control of network slicing and scheduling policies.

Fine-tuning RAN control timers, such as telemetry reporting intervals and action update times, significantly impacts the performance of DRL-based xApps, with smaller time granularities improving eMBB throughput and maintaining mMTC performance.

Reward design and weight configurations in DRL agents influence the trade-offs between competing network slices, with tailored configurations enabling balanced performance across eMBB, mMTC, and URLLC slices.

Hierarchical decision-making with multiple xApps operating at different timescales can improve network performance by balancing the optimization of slicing and scheduling policies for diverse traffic and channel conditions.

DRL agents trained using the PandORA framework demonstrate robust performance in both in-sample and out-of-sample scenarios, including static and mobile environments, while maintaining high resource utilization and slice-specific quality of service requirements.

anchor_claims.text: An intelligent power control algorithm model based on deep neural networks and deep reinforcement learning was developed and demonstrated to improve spectrum resource utilization in a cognitive radio network with one primary user and one secondary user.

The deep Q-network algorithm based on deep reinforcement learning achieves faster convergence and higher success rates compared to the traditional distributed clustering and power control algorithm in wireless communication scenarios.

The proposed algorithm model enables secondary users to share spectrum resources with primary users without causing harmful interference, achieving a success rate of 1 under different power control strategies.
The first power control strategy outperforms the second in terms of loss function changes, success rate, and average transmission times, while both strategies achieve a success rate close to 100%.

**Summary: Deep Neural Networks and Deep Reinforcement Learning for Wireless Communication Optimization and Resource Allocation**

Advances in deep neural networks (DNNs) and deep reinforcement learning (DRL) have catalyzed significant progress in optimizing resource allocation and performance in wireless communication systems. Across a spectrum of network architectures—from cognitive radio and vehicular (V2X) networks to 5G, 6G, and massive MIMO—these AI-driven approaches address fundamental challenges such as spectrum utilization, interference management, latency reduction, and energy efficiency.

DNN-based models, including convolutional and graph neural networks, excel at capturing complex spatial, temporal, and topological patterns in radio environments to improve channel modeling and feature extraction. When integrated with DRL techniques—such as Q-learning, Deep Q-Networks (DQN), Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), and federated learning—these frameworks learn optimal policies for dynamic, often non-convex, resource allocation tasks. This includes joint optimization of power control, beamforming, scheduling, bandwidth allocation, and service differentiation among network slices.

Notably, DRL algorithms, including DDQN and federated variants, demonstrate superior convergence speed, robustness to dynamic channel conditions, and improved metrics like latency, throughput, energy efficiency, and system fairness compared to traditional heuristic or distributed algorithms. In Open RAN environments, automated frameworks like PandORA enable the design, training, and evaluation of DRL-based xApps to fine-tune operational parameters and balance competing quality-of-service (QoS) requirements for diverse user classes (e.g., eMBB, URLLC, mMTC). 

In cognitive radio networks, DNN+DRL approaches have been shown to enable secondary users to share spectrum with primaries without causing interference while achieving high success rates, leveraging adaptive power control and spectrum access strategies. For vehicular networks, joint allocation of bandwidth and power using GNN-DQN frameworks enhances V2V and V2I communication, managing interference and improving reliability even under high mobility and density. 

Federated and multi-agent learning further extend these benefits by addressing privacy concerns and enabling distributed optimization, which is crucial in large-scale, heterogeneous wireless deployments (e.g., 5G-V2X, mobile edge computing, IoT). These methods demonstrate scalability, low latency, and improved generalization in dynamic environments. Challenges remain in computational complexity, data scarcity, and the need for secure, privacy-preserving learning—however, ongoing research continues to bridge these gaps, positioning deep neural network– and deep reinforcement learning–based approaches as transformative for next-generation wireless resource management.

**Summary: Deep Neural Networks and Deep Reinforcement Learning for Wireless Communication Optimization – Resource Allocation**

This body of research explores the synergistic use of deep neural networks (DNNs) and deep reinforcement learning (DRL) in the optimization and resource allocation of wireless communication systems. Across multiple studies, a consistent theme emerges: the integration of DNNs excels at extracting and modeling complex spatial, temporal, and contextual features from high-dimensional and dynamic wireless data, while DRL provides adaptive, policy-based decision-making that learns optimal resource allocation strategies through interaction with the communication environment.

In cognitive radio networks and multi-user systems (including primary-secondary user setups), DNN-based models have been employed to design intelligent power control and spectrum-sharing algorithms that enhance spectrum resource utilization and minimize interference. Deep Q-Network (DQN), Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), and variants such as Double DQN and Federated DQN are frequently deployed to achieve faster convergence, higher success rates, and better performance than conventional distributed algorithms or heuristic approaches in tasks like power control, beamforming, and scheduling.

Reinforcement learning frameworks often leverage multi-objective optimization to simultaneously maximize metrics such as throughput, energy efficiency, latency, and user fairness. For example, hierarchical reinforcement learning architectures separate high-level admission and resource decisions from low-level task or power allocation, enabling robust handling of complex network dynamics and scalability to large systems (such as maritime or vehicular networks). Multi-agent and federated reinforcement learning approaches further address privacy, data scarcity, and decentralized operation, allowing distributed learning without raw data sharing.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) are integrated with DRL to model non-Euclidean network topologies (e.g., vehicular ad-hoc networks or network slicing), improving the capture of local and global dependencies for efficient resource allocation. In massive MIMO and Ultra-Reliable Low Latency Communication (URLLC), DRL with PPO or TD3 dynamically manage power, user scheduling, and antenna activation to maximize energy and spectral efficiency while maintaining ultra-reliable transmission. These methods also demonstrate robustness to environmental changes, such as channel fading and user mobility.

Beyond single-network scenarios, DRL and DNNs are applied to distributed, federated, and edge-centric architectures (such as 5G-V2X, MEC, and O-RAN), enabling real-time adaptation and optimized resource allocation for heterogeneous and highly dynamic environments. Federated DRL models address scalability and privacy in IoT and edge computing, while priority-aware and hierarchical RL frameworks ensure service differentiation for different application classes (e.g., URLLC vs. eMBB). 

Challenges remain, including computational complexity, scalability to massive networks, data scarcity for training, and robustness to interference and adversarial conditions. Still, the overall evidence supports that combining DNNs for feature extraction and representation with DRL for policy optimization offers a powerful, versatile approach to enhance wireless communication performance—particularly in improving resource utilization, reliability, latency, and multi-slice QoS through complex, dynamic wireless environments.

**Summary:**

Recent research at the intersection of deep neural networks (DNN), deep reinforcement learning (DRL), and wireless communication has focused on the dynamic optimization of network resources. Numerous studies demonstrate that hybrid approaches leveraging both DNNs and DRL can significantly enhance performance across various wireless communication scenarios. 

Key advancements include the development of intelligent power control algorithms and resource allocation frameworks that use DNNs for feature extraction and DRL (especially Deep Q-Networks, Proximal Policy Optimization, Soft Actor-Critic, and Federated DRL) to adaptively and optimally manage spectrum, transmit power, bandwidth, and scheduling decisions. These methods have shown superiority in improving metrics such as throughput, energy efficiency, latency, and spectral utilization compared to traditional optimization, heuristic, or centralized approaches.

These DNN-DRL methods tackle multi-objective optimization problems—simultaneously improving throughput, energy efficiency, user fairness, and QoS while adapting to channel dynamics, interference, and user mobility. The use of adaptive reward functions and policy optimization frameworks allows the systems to handle real-time decision making in the presence of non-ideal conditions (e.g., interference, jamming, resource constraints).

Applications span cognitive and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), massive MIMO, network slicing (for differentiated services like eMBB, mMTC, URLLC), and even Open RAN architectures, where automated DRL agent design and evaluation platforms (such as PandORA) facilitate experimentation and deployment. Despite promising results, challenges remain regarding computational complexity, scalability, training data requirements, and robustness to distribution shifts in real-world networks.

In summary, the integration of deep neural networks for data representation and deep reinforcement learning for autonomous decision-making represents a powerful paradigm for optimizing resource allocation and performance in modern wireless communication systems, offering substantial gains in efficiency, adaptability, and service quality.

This body of research explores the synergistic use of deep neural networks (DNNs) and deep reinforcement learning (DRL) in the optimization and resource allocation of wireless communication systems. Across multiple studies, a consistent theme emerges: the integration of DNNs excels at extracting and modeling complex spatial, temporal, and contextual features from high-dimensional and dynamic wireless data, while DRL provides adaptive, policy-based decision-making that learns optimal resource allocation strategies through interaction with the communication environment.

In cognitive radio networks and multi-user systems (including primary-secondary user setups), DNN-based models have been employed to design intelligent power control and spectrum-sharing algorithms that enhance spectrum resource utilization and minimize interference. Reinforcement learning frameworks often leverage multi-objective optimization to simultaneously maximize metrics such as throughput, energy efficiency, latency, and user fairness. For example, hierarchical reinforcement learning architectures separate high-level admission and resource decisions from low-level task or power allocation, enabling robust handling of complex network dynamics and scalability to large systems (such as maritime or vehicular networks). Multi-agent and federated reinforcement learning approaches further address privacy, data scarcity, and decentralized operation, allowing distributed learning without raw data sharing.

Below is a synthesized summary of the provided studies, focusing specifically on how deep neural networks (DNNs) and deep reinforcement learning (DRL) are used for wireless communication optimization and resource allocation.

Summary

Deep neural networks and deep reinforcement learning are emerging as powerful approaches for adaptive resource allocation and optimization in wireless communication networks, particularly where conventional mathematical optimization becomes computationally expensive because of mobility, interference, heterogeneous traffic, large state spaces, and rapidly changing channel conditions. Across the studies provided, DNNs are primarily used to learn complex network representations and approximate optimization functions, while DRL enables agents to learn resource-allocation policies directly through interaction with dynamic wireless environments.

A major application is joint radio-resource optimization, including transmit-power control, spectrum and channel allocation, bandwidth scheduling, beamforming, antenna activation, and interference management. DQN, DDQN, PPO, SAC, TD3, and DDPG-based approaches repeatedly demonstrate the ability to optimize such decisions while satisfying constraints related to throughput, latency, reliability, energy consumption, and Quality of Service (QoS). For example, DRL-based power-control approaches enable cognitive-radio secondary users to reuse spectrum while controlling interference to primary users. In Massive MIMO and UAV-assisted cellular systems, DRL jointly optimizes power, scheduling, beamforming, and related resources to balance spectral efficiency and energy efficiency.

DRL is especially valuable for multi-objective resource allocation. Rather than optimizing an isolated network metric, reward functions can combine throughput, spectrum efficiency, energy consumption, latency, reliability, fairness, or semantic performance. This enables agents to dynamically identify useful operating trade-offs. Optimization-theory-assisted DRL further improves this approach by analytically simplifying portions of difficult optimization problems and applying learning only to the remaining decision variables, potentially reducing training requirements and computational complexity while approaching conventional optimization performance.

Resource allocation for network slicing, O-RAN, and cloud-native wireless systems represents another important direction. DDQN, PPO, and TD3 agents dynamically distribute power, bandwidth, scheduling blocks, and computing resources among eMBB, URLLC, and other network slices. O-RAN xApps demonstrate how DRL can support near-real-time resource control, while work on automated DRL frameworks highlights the importance of reward design, telemetry intervals, control timescales, and hierarchical decision-making. These results suggest that successful practical deployment depends not only on the learning algorithm but also on integration with the network's control architecture.

The studies also demonstrate significant applications in vehicular, RIS-assisted, and high-mobility networks. SAC-based resource allocation jointly determines channel sharing, transmit power, and RIS phase shifts to reduce Age of Information and improve V2V transmission reliability. GNNs combined with DDQN provide an additional advantage by representing changing communication and interference relationships as graphs. Vehicles can consequently extract compact information from neighboring nodes and make distributed resource decisions despite changes in network topology and vehicle density.

Similarly, MEC and computation offloading extend resource allocation beyond radio resources. DRL jointly optimizes offloading, server selection, computing resources, power, and communication channels to reduce latency and energy consumption. Federated DRL further distributes policy learning among edge devices while aggregating learned model parameters rather than raw data. Across the supplied work, this architecture is associated with improved scalability and privacy and reduced centralized data exchange. Hierarchical DRL provides another scalable approach by decomposing complex decisions such as virtual-network admission and resource placement into interacting higher- and lower-level policies.

More specialized applications demonstrate the versatility of the paradigm. Game-guided DRL combines Stackelberg-game reasoning with reinforcement learning for anti-jamming channel and power allocation in integrated sensing and communication systems. Semantic-aware DRL optimizes resources according to semantic information delivery rather than conventional bit-level throughput alone. GNN-DRL architectures support topology-aware allocation for V2X and MEC systems, while hybrid neural-network and optimization frameworks attempt to combine the approximation capability of deep learning with explicit mathematical structure.

Overall, the literature indicates a transition from static, model-driven optimization toward adaptive, learning-assisted wireless resource management. The strongest trend is not simply replacing conventional optimization with a neural network, but developing hybrid architectures that combine DNN representation learning, DRL sequential decision-making, optimization theory, graph learning, federated learning, game theory, and domain-specific wireless constraints. These approaches consistently target better resource utilization, throughput, reliability, latency, energy efficiency, interference management, and scalability.

similar_papers.title: Analysis of the role and robustness of artificial intelligence in commodity image recognition under deep learning neural network
similar_papers.abstract: In order to explore the application of the image recognition model based on multi-stage convolutional neural network (MS-CNN) in the deep learning neural network in the intelligent recognition of commodity images and the recognition performance of the method, in the study, the features of color, shape, and texture of commodity images are first analyzed, and the basic structure of deep convolutional neural network (CNN) model is analyzed. Then, 50,000 pictures containing different commodities are constructed to verify the recognition effect of the model. Finally, the MS-CNN model is taken as the research object for improvement to explore the influence of label errors (p = 0.03, 0.05, 0.07, 0.09, 0.12) with different parameter settings and different probabilities (size of convolutional kernel, Dropout rate) on the recognition accuracy of MS-CNN model, at the same time, a CIR system platform based on MS-CNN model is built, and the recognition performance of salt and pepper noise images with different SNR (0, 0.03, 0.05, 0.07, 0.1) was compared, then the performance of the algorithm in the actual image recognition test was compared. The results show that the recognition accuracy is the highest (97.8%) when the convolution kernel size in the MS-CNN model is 2*2 and 3*3, and the average recognition accuracy is the highest (97.8%) when the dropout rate is 0.1; when the error probability of picture label is 12%, the recognition accuracy of the model constructed in this study is above 96%. Finally, the commodity image database constructed in this study is used to identify and verify the model. The recognition accuracy of the algorithm in this study is significantly higher than that of the Minitch stochastic gradient descent algorithm under different SNR conditions, and the recognition accuracy is the highest when SNR = 0 (99.3%). The test results show that the model proposed in this study has good recognition effect in the identification of commodity images in scenes of local occlusion, different perspectives, different backgrounds, and different light intensity, and the recognition accuracy is 97.1%. To sum up, the CIR platform based on MS-CNN model constructed in this study has high recognition accuracy and robustness, which can lay a foundation for the realization of subsequent intelligent commodity recognition technology.

claims.text: A multi-stage convolutional neural network (MS-CNN) model achieves high recognition accuracy and robustness for commodity image recognition, even under conditions of local occlusion, varying perspectives, different backgrounds, and varying light intensities.

The MS-CNN model demonstrates improved recognition accuracy and robustness when using convolution kernel sizes of 2x2 and 3x3 and a Dropout rate of 0.1, achieving an average recognition accuracy of 97.8%.
The MS-CNN model maintains a recognition accuracy above 96% even when the error probability of image labels reaches 12%, indicating its robustness to labeling errors.

The MS-CNN model outperforms the Minitch stochastic gradient descent algorithm in recognition accuracy under varying signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions, demonstrating superior generalization and robustness.

The MS-CNN-based commodity image recognition platform significantly outperforms traditional models like SIFT, VGG19, and ResNet in both recall rate and accuracy for single and multiple commodity image recognition tasks.

similar_papers.title: The Analysis of Plants Image Recognition Based on Deep Learning and Artificial Neural Network
similar_papers.abstract: Classification and identification of plants are helpful for people to effectively understand and protect plants. The leaves of plants are the most important recognition organs. With the development of artificial intelligence and machine vision technology, plant leaf recognition technology based on image analysis is used to improve the knowledge of plant classification and protection. Deep learning is the abbreviation of deep neural network learning method and belongs to neural network structure. It can automatically learn features from big data and use artificial neural network based on back propagation algorithm to train and classify plant leaf samples. The main content of this paper is to extract plant leaf features and identify plant species based on image analysis. Firstly, plant leaf images are segmented by various methods, and then feature extraction algorithm is used to extract leaf shape and texture features from leaf sample images. Then the comprehensive characteristic information of plant leaves is formed according to the comprehensive characteristic information. In this paper, 50 plant leaf databases are tested and compared with KNN-based neighborhood classification, Kohonen network based on self-organizing feature mapping algorithm and SVM-based support vector machine. At the same time, the leaves of 7 different plants were compared and it was found that ginkgo leaves were easier to identify. For leaf images under complex background, good recognition effect has been achieved. Image samples of the test set are input into the learning model to obtain reconstruction errors. The class label of the test set can be obtained by reconstructing the deep learning model with the smallest error set. The results show that this method has the shortest recognition time and the highest correct recognition rate.

claims.text: Plant leaf recognition based on image analysis can be effectively achieved by extracting shape and texture features using segmentation methods such as threshold, edge, and region segmentation.

Artificial neural networks using backpropagation algorithms demonstrate higher recognition accuracy and shorter recognition time compared to KNN, Kohonen networks, and SVM for plant leaf classification.
Combining shape and texture features into feature vectors improves the recognition rate of plant leaves compared to using texture features alone.
Deep learning models with hierarchical convolutional layers can extract global and contextual features from plant leaf images, enabling accurate classification even in complex backgrounds.

The application of artificial neural networks for plant leaf recognition is effective across diverse plant species and does not require manual feature selection or background removal, making it suitable for real-world scenarios.

similar_papers.title: Efficacy of Two Hidden Layers Artificial Neural Network Synapticity for Deep Learning: A Case of Pattern Recognition
similar_papers.abstract: Most research works in Artificial Neural Network (ANN) are accustomed with the use of single hidden layer (SHL) topology without giving considerations to the problem type, its complexity and desired depth of supervised or unsupervised learning. This could be partly due to the inherent complexities associated with the use of more than one hidden layer which in turn affects solution efficiency. However, the trade-off occasionally is between efficiency and effectiveness of result. When effectiveness is prioritized perhaps for sensitive or mission critical systems, then multiple hidden layers can become advantageous. This research has investigated the ability of an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) with two hidden layer topology to exhibit deep learning behaviour in comparison with a single hidden layer architecture ANN system. A two hidden layer (THL) Neural Network was developed and implemented using Microsoft Visual Studio programming suite and applied to a pattern recognition problem. The gradient descent optimization of the back propagation algorithm in a feed forward scheme was used in the development of the supervised ANN which consisted of thirty inputs at the input layer, two hidden layers with five nodes and a single output layer with one node for a Boolean response. Normalized images mapped into a pattern extraction template using principal component analysis (PCA) of the original images served as pre-processed inputs to the two hidden layer architecture with an initial learning rate of η = 0.1 and maximum tolerable rate of η = 0.4 for fast convergence. Iterations for validation of the feed forward back propagation algorithm using three image patterns showed that over 96% recognition of presented data was recorded. Graphical comparison of the results obtained from separate iterative sessions of the One Hidden Layer (OHL) and (THL) architectures under same input-output dataset revealed more visible traits of attained deep learning by the two hidden layer architecture due to enhanced synapticity of additional nodes.

claims.text: A two hidden layer artificial neural network (ANN) architecture demonstrates improved deep learning performance and pattern recognition capabilities compared to a single hidden layer ANN, particularly in tasks involving complex and large-scale data patterns.

The enhanced synapticity provided by the two hidden layer ANN topology allows for better feature extraction and validation, leading to higher recognition rates in pattern recognition tasks when pre-normalized inputs are used.

The use of principal component analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction and feature extraction improves the performance of artificial neural networks in pattern recognition tasks by providing pre-normalized inputs.

Gradient descent optimization in a two hidden layer ANN, with varying learning rates, achieves effective convergence and improved learning outcomes compared to a single hidden layer ANN under the same input-output conditions.

The two hidden layer ANN architecture is particularly effective in applications such as hurricane trajectory prediction, nomadic movement analysis, and medical image diagnosis, demonstrating its versatility in handling diverse real-world pattern recognition problems.

Self-supervised learning and contrastive learning provide optimization paths for feature representation by leveraging unlabeled data and constructing discriminative feature spaces, enhancing performance in scenarios with limited labeled data.

similar_papers.title: Analysis of tuberculosis detection using deep learning technique and explainable artificial intelligence
similar_papers.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) affects the health of many individuals and is still a prime worldwide health concern despite having so many advanced treatments, as it still lacks technical advancement in its treatment and diagnosis. Accuracy in identification and early detection is essential to reduce the spread and improve treatment outcomes. Traditional methods of diagnosis, such as sputum microscopy and culture, are labor-dependent and subject to human mistakes as it is done by lab technicians. Recent improvements in deep learning have demonstrated significant potential for enhancing and automating diagnostic accuracy. Our research proposes a deep learning based technique that detects TB from chest X-rays after image processing techniques like augmentation. After training on big data, our model pulls off an astonishing accuracy of 97.42% and a loss of 7.17%, outperforming traditional methods. The model uses convolutional neural network (CNN) as a base and transfer learning method, like DenseNet-121, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) technique, like Grad-CAM, to recognize TB related patterns effectively and with low false positives. This approach has the ability to revolutionize the diagnosis of TB and offer more dependable, scalable, and timely solutions to healthcare systems worldwide.

similar_papers.title: Unveiling the Power of Deep Learning: Insights into Advanced Neural n Network Architectures
similar_papers.abstract: Deep learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm within artificial intelligence, revolutionizing various fields with its ability to automatically discover intricate patterns and representations from vast amounts of data. In this article, we delve into the latest advancements in deep learning, focusing on the exploration of advanced neural network architectures. Through a comprehensive review and analysis, we uncover the underlying principles and methodologies driving the success of these architectures, elucidating their capabilities and limitations. From convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image recognition to recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for sequential data processing, we highlight key innovations and breakthroughs that have propelled the field forward. Furthermore, we discuss recent trends such as attention mechanisms, transformer models, and graph neural networks, showcasing their potential applications and impact across diverse domains. By unraveling the power of deep learning and its advanced neural network architectures, this article aims to provide valuable insights into the state-of-the-art techniques driving AI research and development.

similar_papers.title: Research on Image Recognition Technology Based on Deep Learning
similar_papers.abstract: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence technology, image recognition technology is playing an increasingly important role in fields such as healthcare, security, and autonomous driving. Traditional image recognition methods have limited recognition accuracy and generalization ability in complex scenarios, while the introduction of deep learning technology has greatly promoted progress in this field. This paper mainly studies image recognition technology based on deep learning, including a review of traditional methods, the evolution of new technologies, the development process of deep learning in image recognition, and the optimization directions of existing technologies. This paper also explores how deep learning can enhance the performance of image recognition, analyzes its technical advantages, and explores possible directions for improvement. The study employed the methods of literature review and comparative analysis. By collating academic papers, industry reports, and technical cases from the past, it compared the performance differences between traditional methods and deep learning methods, and analyzed the applications of typical deep learning models in image recognition. This paper finds that deep learning significantly improves the accuracy and robustness of image recognition, but still faces challenges such as strong data dependence and high computational cost. Future research can focus on lightweight models, small sample learning, and multimodal fusion.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) excel in image recognition by automatically learning hierarchical feature representations, enabling superior generalization across diverse tasks compared to handcrafted feature descriptors.
Emerging hybrid approaches that combine traditional feature-engineered methods like SIFT with deep learning models demonstrate improved precision and interpretability in image recognition tasks.

Future research in image recognition should focus on lightweight models, few-shot or self-supervised learning, multimodal fusion, and the application of explainable AI to address current limitations in data dependency and computational efficiency.

similar_papers.title: CONVOLUTIONAL DEEP LEARNING NEURAL NETWORK FOR STROKE IMAGE RECOGNITION: REVIEW
similar_papers.abstract: . Deep learning is one of the developing area of artiﬁcial intelligence research. It includes artiﬁcial neural network-based machine learning approaches. One method that has been widely used and researched in recent years is convolution neural networks (CNN). Convolutional neural networks have diﬀerent research issues and medicine is one of the main ones. Today, the predominant global problem is acute cerebral blood ﬂow disorder - stroke. The most important diagnostic tests for stroke are computerized tomography (CT) imaging and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). However, late recognition and diagnosis by a specialist can aﬀect the lives of many patients. For such cases, the role and help of convolutional neural networks are extraordinary. In-depth clustering neural networks apply non-linear transformations and abstractions of high-level models in large databases. Year after year, advances in the ﬁeld of deep learning architecture, namely crate neural networks for the recognition of stroke, are making an important contribution to medicine’s evolution. In this paper, a review of the achievements of deep learning neural networks in the recognition of stroke from brain images is considered. This review chronologically presents the main neural network block diagram and open databases providing MRI and CT images. In addition, a comparative analysis of convolutional neural networks are used in this study of stroke detection is exhibited, in addition achieved indicators of the methodologies used.

Publicly available datasets, such as ISLES, BraTS, and the International Stroke Database, provide essential resources for training convolutional neural networks in stroke detection and segmentation tasks.

Advances in convolutional neural network architectures have significantly contributed to the development of automated diagnostic systems for stroke, aiding medical professionals in timely and accurate decision-making.

similar_papers.title: DeepHeartCT: A fully automatic artificial intelligence hybrid framework based on convolutional neural network and multi-atlas segmentation for multi-structure cardiac computed tomography angiography image segmentation
similar_papers.abstract: Cardiac computed tomography angiography (CTA) is an emerging imaging modality for assessing coronary artery as well as various cardiovascular structures. Recently, deep learning (DL) methods have been successfully applied to many applications of medical image analysis including cardiac CTA structure segmentation. However, DL requires a large amounts of data and high-quality labels for training which can be burdensome to obtain due to its labor-intensive nature. In this study, we aim to develop a fully automatic artificial intelligence (AI) system, named DeepHeartCT, for accurate and rapid cardiac CTA segmentation based on DL. The proposed system was trained using a large clinical dataset with computer-generated labels to segment various cardiovascular structures including left and right ventricles (LV, RV), left and right atria (LA, RA), and LV myocardium (LVM). This new system was trained directly using high-quality computer labels generated from our previously developed multi-atlas based AI system. In addition, a reverse ranking strategy was proposed to assess the segmentation quality in the absence of manual reference labels. This strategy allowed the new framework to assemble optimal computer-generated labels from a large dataset for effective training of a deep convolutional neural network (CNN). A large clinical cardiac CTA studies (n = 1,064) were used to train and validate our framework. The trained model was then tested on another independent dataset with manual labels (n = 60). The Dice score, Hausdorff distance and mean surface distance were used to quantify the segmentation accuracy. The proposed DeepHeartCT framework yields a high median Dice score of 0.90 [interquartile range (IQR), 0.90–0.91], a low median Hausdorff distance of 7 mm (IQR, 4–15 mm) and a low mean surface distance of 0.80 mm (IQR, 0.57–1.29 mm) across all segmented structures. An additional experiment was conducted to evaluate the proposed DL-based AI framework trained with a small vs. large dataset. The results show our framework also performed well when trained on a small optimal training dataset (n = 110) with a significantly reduced training time. These results demonstrated that the proposed DeepHeartCT framework provides accurate and rapid cardiac CTA segmentation that can be readily generalized for handling large-scale medical imaging applications.
